title: Esther 2:19–23
context: When the virgins are gathered a second time, Mordecai is sitting in the king’s gate. Esther has still not made known her relatives or her people, as Mordecai commanded, and she continues to obey him as she did when he brought her up. While he sits in the gate, two doorkeepers, Bigthan and Teresh, grow angry and seek to lay hands on the king. The plot becomes known to Mordecai; he tells Esther, and she tells the king in Mordecai’s name. The matter is investigated, found true, and the two are hanged on a gallows; the affair is written in the book of the chronicles in the king’s presence. What the second gathering was, and what office the king’s gate implies, are not explained in detail and should be left modest. The concealment is still narrative, still under Mordecai’s command, and still not a place to invent a party contrast; moral comment remains hedged, as at 2:10. The book never names God. That an unrewarded report, written down, will later matter is a common hidden-providence reading of the book’s shape, shared in both traditions and to be held with a light hand, not treated as a secret message in the chronicles notice itself. Both traditions close the chapter on a real plot discovered and recorded, the queen still silent about her people.

verses.text: When the virgins were gathered together the second time, Mordecai was sitting in the king’s gate.
verses.arminianNotes:
“When the virgins were gathered together the second time, Mordecai was sitting in the king’s gate.” The second gathering is stated without an explanation: it may continue the earlier collection, or it may be another assembly; the verse does not say, and no choice among those readings is made here. Mordecai sits in the king’s gate, a place of public business in the story, though his exact office is not given here.

Arminian readers take the gate as a real post of watching and access, Mordecai present at the court where the next plot will surface.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the second gathering unexplained and the gate as the narrative locates him, a public place beside the palace, not a title to be filled in.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the gathering or the gate, and they do not force a meaning the verse withholds.

verses.text: Esther had not yet made known her relatives nor her people, as Mordecai had commanded her; for Esther obeyed Mordecai, like she did when she was brought up by him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Esther had not yet made known her relatives nor her people, as Mordecai had commanded her; for Esther obeyed Mordecai, like she did when she was brought up by him.” The concealment continues after she is queen, still under his command, and the verse adds her ongoing obedience, like her life in his house. As at 2:10, the book reports this without a verdict. Hedged evaluations of prudence or unease may be found within both traditions; they are not a fork between the traditions, and none should be invented here.

Arminian readers take the continued silence and the continued obedience as real, a queen still listening to the man who raised her, without settling the ethics of the concealment in this line.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear the same delay: her people are not yet made known, and she obeys Mordecai as before. Later pressure will come; this verse only keeps the secret in place.

Both traditions refuse a party contrast over the concealment and keep any moral comment modest.

verses.text: In those days, while Mordecai was sitting in the king’s gate, two of the king’s eunuchs, Bigthan and Teresh, who were doorkeepers, were angry, and sought to lay hands on the King Ahasuerus.
verses.arminianNotes:
While Mordecai is sitting in the king’s gate, “two of the king’s eunuchs, Bigthan and Teresh, who were doorkeepers, were angry, and sought to lay hands on the King Ahasuerus.” A plot against the king is named, with two servants and a stated anger. Their reasons are not given, and they are not invented here. The danger is real inside the court where Esther now reigns, her people still unknown.

Arminian readers take the intended attack as a historical conspiracy, two doorkeepers seeking to harm the king, the event on which the next verses turn.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep Bigthan and Teresh as named doorkeepers whose anger leads to a plot, a fact of the court, not a symbol of a later enemy.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the anger and do not fill in a motive the verse leaves closed.

verses.text: This thing became known to Mordecai, who informed Esther the queen; and Esther informed the king in Mordecai’s name.
verses.arminianNotes:
“This thing became known to Mordecai, who informed Esther the queen; and Esther informed the king in Mordecai’s name.” The news reaches Mordecai; he tells the queen; she tells the king and gives Mordecai the credit. The chain is simple and public in its last step. How the plot became known to him is not explained.

Arminian readers take the warning as a real, responsible act: Mordecai speaks, Esther speaks in his name, a human loyalty that will save the king’s life.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also trace the same chain, the queen using her access in Mordecai’s name. That the book does not name God here does not prove absence, and it does not turn the report into a coded sign. A later providence reading of this unrewarded loyalty belongs to the story’s shape, shared and hedged.

Both traditions keep the verse as a discovery and a faithful report, without a party contrast.

verses.text: When this matter was investigated, and it was found to be so, they were both hanged on a gallows; and it was written in the book of the chronicles in the king’s presence.
verses.arminianNotes:
The matter is investigated and found to be so; “they were both hanged on a gallows; and it was written in the book of the chronicles in the king’s presence.” The two are executed, and the record is entered while the king is there. Mordecai is not rewarded in this chapter. Readers in both traditions often look ahead to the later night when this very record will be read; that reading of the book’s shape is common and may be named, but it is not a hidden sentence in this verse, and it remains shared ground, not a new contrast.

Arminian readers take the hanging and the written record as the real close of the plot, a public finding and a public death, with Mordecai’s name now in the chronicles.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also stay with the investigation, the gallows, and the book of the chronicles. The entry is made in the king’s presence, and it will stand until a later chapter returns to it.

Both traditions close the unit on that written notice, still without naming God, still without treating the silence as absence, and still without a keyContrast over providence or over Esther’s hidden people.
